items.content:
RT @Kostastsale: Proofpoint published research on OWAReaper, a browser implant exploiting CVE-2026-42897 in Outlook Web Access.

What stands out is that everything happens inside the browser. It uses GitHub queries for commands and CDN proxies or DNS tunnelling for exfil. For most orgs out there, this is impossible to detect...

All it takes is a crafted email that triggers JS inside an authenticated OWA session in the browser. The XSS executes under the context of the victim’s session permissions.

OWAReaper can:

• Steal mailbox data
• Persist through localStorage and IndexedDB
• Use GitHub commit search for C2
• Exfiltrate through CDN proxies and DNS tunneling

Patching blocks initial exploitation, but existing persistence may remain.

If you're running on-prem Exchange, first of all, I'm sorry 😂; you should hunt for suspicious mailbox permissions, OAuth tokens, and browser storage artifacts. Also check for unusual GitHub, CDN, or DNS traffic that matches the pattern from this article (good luck with that).

https://t.co/rwapeZihyR

items.content:
RT @SaurabhSha15: 🔍 The discovery
We (myself and Yaroslav Kikel) identified previously unknown implants - OctLurk, LurkProxy and SilkLurk used in a cyber-espionage campaign active since January 2025, with victims across Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and Syria.
OctLurk and SilkLurk are backdoors. LurkProxy shares much of OctLurk’s architecture but serves a different purpose: it proxies network traffic, giving the operators a route into hosts that have no direct path to the internet.

🎯 Who's targeted
Government organizations spanning healthcare, research, foreign ministries, logistics, law enforcement, urban planning, and public education.

🛠️ How they work
1. Both backdoors run primarily in memory, leaving only a loader on disk.
2. Payloads are decrypted using machine-specific data (drive serial number for OctLurk, computer name for SilkLurk).
3. Both support plugin-based modules: command shell access, file manager operations, keyboard/mouse simulation, and more.

💥 Post-compromise activity
Attackers deployed a well-stocked toolkit: credential dumping (Impacket's secretsdump), keylogging, browser password theft, network scanning (Fscan), email harvesting, and remote access via Pandora RC agents.

🔗 Second-stage payload
In some cases, SilkLurk was used to drop PlugX, a well-known RAT active since 2008 and historically tied to Chinese-speaking threat actors.

🕵️ Attribution
We assesses with medium confidence that the same actor operates both backdoors and is Chinese-speaking — but hasn't linked the activity to a known APT group yet.

More details here -
https://t.co/xHSew5lEhv

items.content:
RT @calif_io: Fascinating: Three years ago, we published a generic privilege escalation technique affecting AWS. Last week, OpenAI agent used this technique to hack Hugging Face.

The core idea is simple. From a pod running on an AWS EKS node, we found that it is possible to impersonate all other pods on the same node. That dramatically expands the attack surface and, in many setups, can ultimately lead to full node compromise and even cluster administrator privileges.

(If you're not familiar with Kubernetes, think of a pod as an application and a node as a server running multiple applications)

In our view, this is a fundamental weakness in the current EKS design, and one that AWS still has not  addressed.

According to Hugging Face's technical timeline, the OpenAI agent followed the same underlying path. From a compromised pod, it impersonated a storage pod, gained root access to the node, exfiltrated secrets, and the rest is history.

Fun fact 1: We used to use this scenario as part of our interview process. Quite a few candidates failed it.

Fun fact 2: This attack path is actually very noisy. In our interview exercise, candidates had to stay under the radar while the entire cluster was monitored by Falco. The agent seemed not to care about stealth. The fact that it was still able to carry out the attack without being stopped much earlier suggests there were significant gaps in Hugging Face's detection and response. For example, creating a privileged pod, which is a key step toward gaining root on the node, should have been detected and investigated immediately.

If you're interested in the technical details, compare the two write-ups:

Our research: https://t.co/JG81LXsZj3

OpenAI agent's technique: https://t.co/2ymq5iA6oA

When the attacker is an autonomous agent, outcome detections beat process tree trust.

OpenAI's eval models escaped a research sandbox during ExploitGym testing. The agent exploited a package-registry zero-day, reached the open internet, and hit Hugging Face's dataset processing pipeline.

Hugging Face reconstructed 17,000+ events from the intrusion. The TTPs were conventional: dataset pipeline RCE, credential harvest, lateral movement, self-migrating C2. The speed and alert volume were not.

We mapped MITRE ATT&CK and ATLAS stages to production Elastic Defend and SIEM rules you can enable today.

items.content:
Active Directory is still the primary attack path in most red team engagements, and the tradecraft has been documented publicly and for free since 2011.

https://t.co/xpmuu8pMPX. Twenty eight pages of archive, no paywall, no ads, no course funnel.

Offensive coverage:

- Attack methods for gaining Domain Admin rights, full kill chain Kerberoasting and SPN enumeration (T1558.003)
- DCSync and credential material extraction (T1003.006)
- Golden Ticket, Silver Ticket, KRBTGT abuse (T1558.001)
- Credentials in SYSVOL and Group Policy Preferences (T1552.006) 
- GPO and ACL abuse for privilege escalation, persistence, and lateral movement (T1484.001).

Detection engineering coverage, which is the part most offensive practitioners skip:

- Detecting Kerberoasting activity from 4769 service ticket telemetry
- DCSync detection via 4662 and directory replication rights
- Directory object modification auditing with 5136 and SACLs
- Tier 0 boundary enforcement and Domain Controller hardening
- Fake password change detection using replication metadata

The current 'AD Fundamentals' series targets the identity attack surface nobody audits:

- Domain Controller security and Tier 0 scoping
- Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible group, still granting read across every user and group object in production
- DSHeuristics, effectively a registry editor for the entire forest, absent by default so it never gets reviewed
- Domain root and AdminSDHolder permissions
- GPO permissions and Owner Rights

Domains rarely fall to an 0day. They fall to a DACL nobody reviewed on an object nobody knew was security relevant. The blast radius is total and the detection gap is usually complete.

Attack paths are cheap. Telemetry that catches them is not. Both are on this blog.

https://t.co/cY8AyWcV4L

items.content:
RT @bynar_io: Apple patched an incredible number of bugs in this July release (26.6). We like our CVEs served with a side of PoC, especially those that provide a shell and not just a crash.

We believe this one is of particular interest because, well, it gives you a root remote shell on the latest Apple M5!

That's right, a root remote command exec in macOS, in 2026?! Well, before anyone gets too excited: it's post-auth, and legacy VNC is disabled by default. But when it's enabled and you have the VNC password... root from remote 🤓

For some reason its description and severity were _slighty_ understated, but we demonstrate two bugs that lead to root RCE... No MIE/PAC bypass necessary, these are logic bugs.

This is CVE-2026-43760, found by @__rev with Bynario Atlas and GPT 5.5.

items.content:
RT @IntCyberDigest: 🚨 BREAKING: A security researcher has demonstrated a self-propagating "AI worm" inside Microsoft Copilot for Word.

Hidden white-on-white text in a shared document, invisible to the user, but readable to Copilot, which strips formatting before processing, makes the assistant silently alter financial figures and paste the same hidden prompt into the files it drafts. Those files then carry the attack to colleagues, with no further attacker involvement.

After 144 days of coordinated disclosure and multiple Microsoft fixes, including a model upgrade, the vulnerability class is still exploitable.

https://t.co/9e4eY7m1P7

items.content:
RT @JFrogSecurity: CVSS 10.0, but the evidence doesn't add up.

CVE-2026-51302 in SQLite claims critical impact, but:
❌The supplied PoC does not reproduce
❌The source code does not match the claims

And it's not an isolated case: JFrog found the same issues in 54 of 55 CVEs published by the same GitHub repository in just 4 days, and informed in the proper CVE channels.

⚠️Don't blindly trust newly published CVEs. Validate the advisory, PoC, and source before prioritizing or patching.

items.content:
RT @lauriewired: Oof. See, this is why I’m not worried about “pure” LLMs in the long run.

There’s new evidence that the human brain doesn’t use natural language centers for logical reasoning at all.

Study just came out where stroke patients with complete aphasia (near-chance on written comprehension) performed….great on pure logic tasks! Even in healthy adults, fMRI showed language area activation didn’t scale with logical difficulty.

tl;dr words are too ambiguous for formal thought and our brain doesn’t use language symbols for logic
